target: ¿Para qué sirve esto?
english: What is this for?
tip: Two whys: por qué asks the cause, para qué asks the purpose. "¿Para qué sirve esto?" = what is this FOR – swap them and you're asking the wrong question.

target: Ponlo aquí, por favor.
english: Put it here, please.
tip: In 'Ponlo', the pronoun lo attaches to the affirmative command – it goes at the end as one word.

target: ¿Podrías cerrar la ventana?
english: Could you close the window?
tip: "Podrías" = could you? Conditional of poder for polite requests. "¿Podrías ayudarme?" Softer than "¿Puedes...?"

target: Espero que llegues a tiempo.
english: I hope you arrive on time.
tip: Espero que + subjunctive: hoping about someone else's action triggers subjunctive. "Espero que vengas" (I hope you come).

target: Me alegro de que hayas venido.
english: I'm glad you came.
tip: "Me alegro de que" + present perfect subjunctive.

target: Deja de pegarle a tu hermana.
english: Stop hitting your sister.
tip: You don't hit someone in Spanish – you hit TO them: "pegarle a tu hermana" needs le + a, as if delivering the blow. Pegar treats its victim as an indirect object.

target: Es importante que hables con él.
english: It's important that you talk to him.
tip: Es importante que + subjunctive: impersonal value judgments trigger subjunctive. "Es importante que estudies."

target: Puede que tengamos que cancelar la reunión.
english: We might have to cancel the meeting.
tip: Puede que + subjunctive = maybe/it's possible: "Puede que venga" (He might come). Possibility → subjunctive.

target: Yo en tu lugar buscaría otro trabajo.
english: In your place, I would look for another job.
tip: No if-clause required: "Yo en tu lugar" (me, in your place) + conditional "buscaría" does the whole 'if I were you' job. Spanish skips the si entirely.

target: Siga todo recto y gire a la derecha.
english: Go straight ahead and turn right.
tip: Strangers get flipped-vowel orders: usted commands like "siga" and "gire" (from sigue/gira). Directions from officials and shopkeepers always come in this shape.

target: Te lo digo para que no te preocupes.
english: I'm telling you so you don't worry.
tip: "Para que" + subjunctive = so that: "Hablo despacio para que entiendas." Purpose involving another person → subjunctive.

target: A menos que llueva, vamos a la playa.
english: Unless it rains, we're going to the beach.
tip: A menos que always takes subjunctive.

target: No creo que sea tan fácil como parece.
english: I don't think it's as easy as it seems.
tip: No creo que + subjunctive – negated belief triggers subjunctive.

target: El hecho de que no haya venido me preocupa.
english: The fact that he hasn't come worries me.
tip: Even hard facts take subjunctive: "el hecho de que no haya venido" – it really happened, but Spanish marks it as reacted-to, not newly asserted.

target: Lo que quiero saber es si podemos contar contigo.
english: What I want to know is if we can count on you.
tip: 'What' meaning 'the thing that' is lo que: "Lo que quiero saber" = the-thing-that I want to know. Save qué for questions, asked or reported (dime qué...).

target: En caso de que el bebé se despierte, dale el biberón.
english: In case the baby wakes up, give him the bottle.
tip: En caso de que + subjunctive = in case.

target: La reunión de seguimiento se celebrará el próximo lunes a las diez.
english: The follow-up meeting will be held next Monday at ten.
tip: "Se celebrará" isn't about a party: celebrar also means to hold (a meeting, elections, a trial). Here the reunión de seguimiento will simply take place next Monday.

target: No te vayas sin guardar los cambios.
english: Don't leave without saving the changes.
tip: Odd pair: 'go!' is vete, but 'don't go' isn't no te vete – negative commands switch to subjunctive, so it's no te vayas. The pronoun te also jumps back in front.

target: Aunque llueva, vamos a hacer la excursión.
english: Even if it rains, we're going to do the excursion.
tip: Aunque llueva = even if it rains (maybe it won't). Aunque llueve = even though it's raining (it is). One vowel tells you whether the rain is real or hypothetical.

target: Para mí, lo más importante es la familia.
english: For me, the most important thing is family.
tip: "Para mí" = in my opinion: "Para mí, es mejor así." Para + person for personal viewpoint.

target: El restaurante al que fuimos tenía buenas vistas.
english: The restaurant we went to had good views.
tip: English strands prepositions (the restaurant we went TO); Spanish never does. The a jumps up front: "al que fuimos". Saying que fuimos a instantly flags a foreigner.

target: No importa lo lejos que estemos, el vínculo familiar permanece.
english: No matter how far apart we are, the family bond remains.
tip: Lo lejos que estemos – Spanish packages 'how far' as lo + adverb + que, and 'no matter' forces subjunctive estemos: the distance is left open, not stated.

target: Ponme una caña y una ración de croquetas de jamón.
english: Give me a small beer and a portion of ham croquettes.
tip: Bare imperatives are polite bar Spanish: "Ponme una caña" (put me a small draft beer) is standard, not bossy. A could-you-possibly order sounds oddly stiff in Spain.

target: Puse las flores en un jarrón en la mesa del salón.
english: I put the flowers in a vase on the living room table.
tip: The vase trap: flowers go in a "jarrón", never a vaso – vaso is a drinking glass. Ask for a vaso for your roses and you'll get a tumbler of water.

target: El edificio no tiene ascensor y vivimos en el quinto piso.
english: The building has no elevator and we live on the fifth floor.
tip: "El quinto piso" is the US sixth floor: Spanish numbering starts above the planta baja (ground floor). Five full flights with no ascensor – count accordingly.

target: Lo que más me molesta es que no me lo hayan dicho antes.
english: What bothers me the most is that they hadn't told me before.
tip: They really didn't tell – yet it's hayan dicho, subjunctive. Emotion verbs like molestar trigger it even for true facts: you're reacting, not reporting.

target: Haga lo que haga, siempre le critican.
english: Whatever he does, they always criticize him.
tip: Spanish builds 'whatever he does' by echoing the verb: haga lo que haga, literally 'do what he may do'. Works with any verb – diga lo que diga, whatever he says.

target: Haga lo que haga, siempre encuentra algo que criticar.
english: Whatever he does, he always finds something to criticize.
tip: Haga is subjunctive for yo AND él/ella/usted, so haga lo que haga could mean 'whatever I do' or 'whatever he does' – the form alone can't tell you; context has to.

target: No toque eso.
english: Don't touch that.
tip: Tocar is an -ar verb, yet the command is toque: usted commands flip to the opposite vowel (-ar takes -e, -er/-ir take -a). That vowel swap IS the subjunctive.

target: No me lo digas.
english: Don't tell me.
tip: Command someone to do it and pronouns glue onto the verb: dímelo. Say don't and they leap in front: no me lo digas. Negation always pulls pronouns before the verb.
